source_text:
Κατὰ
σύνθεσιν, ὡς ἐπὶ ψυχῆς καὶ σώματος. Καθ' ὑπόστασιν δὲ ἐπὶ μόνης λέγεται τῆς ἐν Χρι
στῷ θεότητος καὶ ἀνθρωπότητος. Ἓν γὰρ πρόσωπον ἔσχον αἱ δύο φύσεις, καὶ οὐ δύο,
κατὰ τὸν λῆρον Νεστόριον.
thought_title: Union according to composition and according to person
orientation: John of Damascus is listing the modes of union and now gives the mode according to composition, then the mode according to person, which he says applies only to Christ's divinity and humanity.
pass_a_gloss: According to composition, as in the case of soul and body. But according to person it is said only of the divinity and humanity in Christ. For the two natures had one person, and not two, according to the nonsense of Nestorius.

choices.why: The preposition κατά with the accusative marks the mode of union being listed; σύνθεσις means a putting together of parts, so composition fits the soul-body example.
The glossary requires person for ὑπόστασις; the phrase names the mode of union, so the same rendering is kept.

choices.term: ἐπὶ μόνης λέγεται τῆς ἐν Χριστῷ θεότητος καὶ ἀνθρωπότητος
choices.english: it is said only of the divinity and humanity in Christ
choices.why: ἐπί with the genitive here means 'in the case of' or 'of'; μόνης is restrictive, so 'only' must be kept; the two natures are named with the article and linked by καί.
rejected: it is spoken upon the sole divinity and humanity in Christ
it applies to the only divinity and humanity in Christ

choices.why: Aorist indicative of ἔχω; the subject is αἱ δύο φύσεις, so the verb is third person plural; the aorist states the fact without ongoing aspect.

choices.english: according to the nonsense of Nestorius
choices.why: κατά with the accusative here means 'according to' or 'in line with'; λῆρος is a strong dismissive noun, so 'nonsense' preserves the polemical tone; Νεστόριον is the accusative of the name.

pass_b_english: Union according to composition is seen in soul and body. Union according to person is spoken of only in the case of the divinity and humanity in Christ. For the two natures had one person, not two, contrary to the nonsense of Nestorius.
